title: K. and the Castle
where: *The Castle*, chapters 1, 2 and 8, in the English of Willa and Edwin Muir (1930)
about: A man the book calls K. comes one night to a snowbound village under a castle and says he is the Land Surveyor the Count is expecting. Next morning he sets out on foot for the Castle: the first passage. That evening a messenger hands him a letter from Klamm, a Castle official: the second. In the third, on his fourth day, K. has waited in an inn yard to catch Klamm at his sleigh, has refused to come away, and is left alone as the lights go out.

view.says: Auden wrote that a typical Kafka story turns the heroic quest upside down. The old hero knows what he must do, and others can tell him the way. Kafka’s hero meets no one who knows it, and K. does not know what he should do. In *The Castle* the letter K. wants to be a word, land-surveyor, and so to have a self like everyone else, and he is not allowed one.
view.source: “The I Without a Self,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 162–63

pair.label: The end of the same paragraph

lenses.label: Clauses
lenses.caption: The second sentence says five things of one street: it does not go up to the Castle hill, makes towards it, turns aside, does not lead away, and gets no nearer. Each new clause takes back part of the last, in Kafka’s German too. One of the translators, Edwin Muir, wrote that Kafka loved a sentence that goes forward, turns back on itself and goes forward again. K. goes on only because he expects the road to come round to the Castle. Auden, writing of the way in the stories typical of Kafka, cites Kafka’s aphorism that there is a goal and no way, and that what is called the way is wavering.
lenses.why: One sentence says five things of a street, each new one taking back part of the last, and ends no nearer the Castle; Auden cites Kafka’s aphorism that there is a goal and no way, only wavering.

lenses.label: Stop

ties.say: The paragraph opens with K. walking again and closes with him at a stop.
The same two words, *go on*: first what he does, then what he cannot do.
In the first passage the way is long. In the second each step is an effort.
K. has to tear himself from the street. In the German it is a street that holds fast.

lenses.caption: Between the two passages K. walks on through a village that seems to have no end. Then he tears himself from the street into a side lane where the snow is deeper, breaks into a sweat, and stops. The two words for what he did, go on, come back after could not. Kafka’s German has one word in both places, weiter, onward, and calls pulling the feet out schwere Arbeit, work that is heavy or hard. No other imagined world, Auden wrote, is as heavy as Kafka’s, and one step in it takes all one’s strength.
lenses.why: The paragraph that starts K. walking ends with him unable to go on, on the same two words; Auden says no imagined world is as heavy as Kafka’s, where one step uses up the strength.

lenses.label: Reading

ties.say: K. counts the form of address among the places that treat him as a free man.
K. counts the mention of his wishes among the places that treat him as a free man.
K. puts this promise with the places that treat him as a minor employee, hardly visible to the heads of departments: keeping him in view takes an effort.
K. adds one word, *only*: his chief is no more than a village official.
And it is to that official that he must answer. K. adds the word *actually*.

lenses.caption: K. finds the letter not consistent and sorts it two ways. The address and the mention of his wishes treat him as a free man. Not to lose sight of him, and a superior who is only a village official, treat him as a minor employee. That the Castle might be undecided hardly occurs to him: he reads the contradiction as a choice left to him. Further on he finds a hint that he made the first move, one only an uneasy conscience would sense: uneasy, the text adds, not bad. Auden wrote that K. cannot take instructions that seem contradictory as a sign of others’ guilt, and that they may prove his own.
lenses.why: K. sorts one letter into words for a free man and words for a minor employee and hardly thinks the Castle undecided; Auden says he cannot read contradictory instructions as guilt in others: they may prove his own.

grounds.claim: which phrases of the letter K. takes up, and to which of the two kinds he puts each

lenses.caption: The letter begins My dear Sir: no name and no title. It takes K. into the Count’s service and speaks of your work without saying what work. The title he came with, Land Surveyor, is not in it, and in chapter 5 the Superintendent tells him that not a word of it shows he was taken on as one. K. himself picks out six of its words, from service to workers, and finds even its personal lines written from an employer’s standpoint. Of this novel Auden wrote that K. wants to be a word, land-surveyor, and so to have a self like everyone else, and that he is not allowed one.
lenses.why: The letter takes K. on for service and work and leaves out the title he claims, as the Superintendent points out; Auden says K. wants to be a word, land-surveyor, and so to have a self, and is not allowed.

turns.what: Woken at the inn, K. says he is the Land Surveyor the Count is expecting.
By telephone the Castle first has no trace of a Land Surveyor. Then it rings back, and the first answer is called a mistake.
K. telephones the Castle as the Land Surveyor’s old assistant. A voice asks what Land Surveyor, then knows of him. Asked when his master may come to the Castle, it answers: never.
Klamm’s letter takes him into the Count’s service and does not use the title.
The Superintendent tells K. that the village does not need a Land Surveyor.
Shown the letter, the Superintendent finds in it no word that K. was taken on as Land Surveyor.
K. accepts the post of school janitor. The teacher who brings the offer says a janitor is needed about as much as a Land Surveyor.
A second letter from Klamm is addressed to the Land Surveyor and praises his surveying. K. says he has done none.
K. tells Olga that his engagement as Land Surveyor was only a pretext.
Erlanger, one of Klamm’s secretaries, sends word that he wants the Land Surveyor at the Herrenhof at once.
The last speech in the text is a question, and its last words are the title.

after the text.what: Kafka never wrote the last chapter. He told his editor how it was to go: K. dies worn out, and word comes from the Castle that he has no valid right to live in the village but may stay and work there.
after the text.source: Max Brod, Additional Note to The Castle, second paragraph, in the Standard Ebooks edition of the Muirs’ translation

lenses.caption: The book calls its hero K. 1,046 times. Its editor, Max Brod, notes that Kafka seems to have begun with I and then put K. in its place. The title K. claims, Land Surveyor, comes 96 times, mostly from people he meets in the village. The Superintendent, whom the letter names as his superior, tells him the village needs no surveyor. Kafka told Brod the ending he never wrote: word comes from the Castle that K. has no valid right to live in the village, but may stay and work there. Auden wrote that the letter K. wants to be a word, land-surveyor, and is not allowed to be one.

lenses.label: Turn
lenses.caption: One main verb, seemed, carries four clauses, each led by as if. Three say what staying has brought K.: the others have broken with him, he is freer than ever, and no one dares touch him. Then comes but, and the fourth, which a remark between dashes rates at least as strong: nothing is more senseless or hopeless than this. So the freedom and its hopelessness are both what seemed to him. Kafka’s German has its as if three times; the Muirs add one. Auden wrote that Kafka’s hero feels imprisoned and tries to get out, but that prison may be the state he was made for, and freedom the thing that would destroy him.
lenses.why: One verb, seemed, carries both the freedom K. has won and the judgment that nothing is more hopeless, rated at least as strong; Auden says prison may be what Kafka’s hero was made for, and freedom what would destroy him.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word or words at the head of phrase after phrase
lenses.caption: The sentence ends on three nouns, each with this before it, after nothing more said twice; Kafka’s German has both repetitions. A word repeated at the head of phrase after phrase is called anaphora, and here it lines the three nouns up as a list. Each names again something the first half gave K.: he was freer, he could wait, and nobody dared touch him. Inviolability is the state of what cannot be injured; Kafka’s word, Unverletzlichkeit, is built on the verb that means to wound. So what the first half gave comes back in the same order, and the sentence says nothing is more senseless or more hopeless than these three.
lenses.why: The last three nouns, lined up by a repeated this, name again in order what the sentence gave K., his freedom, his leave to wait and his safety from touch, and the sentence says nothing is more hopeless than these.

grounds.claim: this three times and nothing more twice, each at the head of its phrase; each of the last three nouns answers an earlier clause, in the same order

anaphora: one word or set of words said again at the start of each clause, sentence or line in a run; the handbook’s own example is John of Gaunt’s speech in Richard II, where this stands before one noun phrase after another, as a list
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), under anaphora, read on 2026-10-03

auden.says: Donald Pearce took the course and made notes after the lectures. According to them, Auden came to Kafka by way of Descartes, asking which of a man’s several selves is the I that thinks. Of modern writers, he said, Kafka best shows the predicaments of mind and metaphysics, above all in *The Castle*. The book is dressed as a satire on bureaucracy; underneath it is a parable, theological and psychological. For the culture of the twentieth century it is what Dante’s poem was for the fourteenth. He told them to read it with the *Divine Comedy* and Melville in mind, and to ask what K.’s quest is for.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 134–35

auden.says: In the same class Auden put a record on. He said that the second movement of Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto shows best, so far as music can show such a thing, how a man stands to his fate: Ahab to his whale, or K. to his Castle. When the piano defies the orchestra and goes off by itself it is soon lost and hysterical, and it comes back to something like sanity only when it accepts the orchestra again. He ended by asking whether it has found its way back too late.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 136

auden.says: Pearce also sat in on a class of the next semester, in 1942. According to his notes, Auden said that a poet getting in touch with his daemon is like trying to phone a friend whose number one cannot recall and will not look up. Kafka, he said, describes the tie between the village and the Castle in just these terms: a telephone exchange that at times works very well and often fails, or works without reason, with calls that go astray and messages only half made out. He glossed the village as the conscious mind, the Castle as the unconscious, and knew no better analogy for composing a poem.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 155–56
auden.checked: read in the scan of Pearce’s essay, research/auden/pearce.txt, on 2026-10-03; the remark is on p. 155 and its sentence runs on to p. 156 (C_auden_on_works.md gives pp. 154-55). Pearce dates the class on p. 154 (1942) and says he was not enrolled in it. In the scan the thing likened to the telephone call is a poet’s making contact with his daemon; the exchange in The Castle is then called the best analogy he knows for the act of composing, in its first stages at least or even as it goes on

auden.says: In February 1941, the year of the course, Auden reviewed Kafka in *The New Republic*. Asked which artist stands to the present age much as Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe did to their own, he wrote, one would think first of Kafka. The three big novels use the oldest device in literature, the Quest. The Kafka hero is Faust turned the other way round. For K. it is being exceptional that makes the trouble, and to become exceptional is to become reflective, and so to find that what is necessary looks arbitrary. This hero’s predicament, he wrote, is contemporary man’s.
auden.source: “The Wandering Jew,” *The New Republic*, 10 February 1941; reprinted in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 110–13

auden.says: In 1946 Auden wrote an essay called “K.’s Quest.” Bunyan’s pilgrim, he says there, must gain heaven by deserving it. K. can earn no right to the title of Land Surveyor: all he can do is ask the Castle to permit it. He suffers and fails for the very reason that he is an individual. Since he cannot stop being K., he will never become the Land Surveyor that he wishes to be. Auden calls the contradiction comic: K. is one letter, and Land Surveyor sounds much the grander, yet K. is an individual’s name, and land survey only defines an occupation.
auden.source: “K.’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, edited by Angel Flores (1946), pp. 47–52

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden calls Kafka a master, perhaps the greatest, of the pure parable, and says that critics have little of worth to say about parables. A parable’s hero may have a name or be called only K.; the name, the time and the place do not bear on what it means. To find the meaning a reader has to give up standing outside and identify with what he reads, so the meaning differs with every reader. A critic who interprets a parable only shows what it has done to him.
auden.source: “The I Without a Self,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 159–60

auden.says: Max Brod’s life of Kafka, he notes, describes a Czech novel about a village under a castle, in which the castle’s officials are plainly evil. He takes this as a sign that the readers who took the people of Kafka’s Castle for agents of divine grace had it wrong, and he sides with a reading in which its officers are indifferent to good where they are not wicked. Fine as *The Trial* and *The Castle* are, he adds, he thinks Kafka’s best work is in *The Great Wall of China*, a volume written in his last six years.

auden.says: In the same essay he sets Kafka’s hero against the heroes of older quests. Their goal is one that everybody wants, and they are confident of reaching it. His goal is his alone. He is sure from the outset that he will fail, and is doomed all the same to enormous efforts. A wrong guess costs him what a wrong choice would, and he must feel as responsible for it. From the beginning he is an I, and his guilt lies in the bare fact that he exists.

caveats: The English is the Muirs’ translation of 1930, the one Auden’s students read. Where a caption says what Kafka’s German has, the German was read in an edition of 1950 and after. The Muirs worked from the first edition of 1926, which was not compared.

Auden’s sentences about the way, about contradictory instructions, about heaviness and about freedom are said of a typical Kafka story, its hero and its world. He cites none of the three passages shown here. Only his sentence about the letter and the word names *The Castle*.

Auden’s review of 1941, “The Wandering Jew,” and his essay of 1946, “K.’s Quest,” were read here only in search snippets of scanned copies. What he said in class is known from notes a student, Donald Pearce, made afterwards, not from Auden’s own text.

*K.* was counted wherever the initial stands, the possessive included, and *Land Surveyor* wherever the two words stand together. Who is speaking was decided by reading each place, and a few could be sorted another way.

The text printed here stops after eighteen chapters. Kafka left the book unfinished, and later editions print more of it. The ending this page reports is one Kafka described to his editor, Max Brod, and never wrote.
open: No German is shown beside the English. No out-of-copyright German text of Das Schloß is listed in remake/research/D_texts.md or cached for build/tools/original.mjs, so the German was only read, at zeno.org (the pages give their source as Gesammelte Werke, Band 2, Frankfurt a.M. 1950 ff.), and single words of it are cited. The zeno.org pages mark the text as in the public domain (gemeinfrei), so the lead could add it and set Kafka’s own sentences beside the English. Whether the first German edition of 1926, which the Muirs translated, differs in these passages was not checked.

Auden’s “The Wandering Jew” (1941) and “K.’s Quest” (1946) are not in the scans. Everything given from them rests on the extracts in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, which were taken from snippets; the pages inside “K.’s Quest” are approximate.

remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md cites Pearce’s Kafka passages at pp. 134, 134-35 and 154-55. In the scan each page’s number is printed at its foot, and by that the passages are on pp. 135, 136 and 155-56; remake/research/A_michigan_course.md has 135 and 136 as well. The reading uses the pages of the scan.

In The Dyer’s Hand the sentences on the Quest are about “a typical Kafka story” and “the Kafka hero”; the paragraph before them is about the late stories. Auden then speaks of K and names The Trial and The Castle on p. 163. The captions say “Kafka’s hero” where he does.

The Muirs depart from the German in the passages shown: try in the letter is theirs; as if stands four times for als three times; escaped renders a lane that took him in; the obsession of the street renders a street that held him fast; at liberty is added beside freer. In K.’s reading, outside the part shown, they had to be faced renders a German clause that says the contradictions must be intended.

In the third passage word 365 is two words joined by a dash: the end of the remark between dashes and the first word of the fourth as if. Three marks shared it. From the examiner: mended. The span of the remark now ends at 365.1, and the last clause and the fourth as if begin at 365.2.

The 96 uses of the title were sorted by reading each. Schwarzer, Barnabas and the assistants, who all belong to the Castle in some way, are counted with the people K. meets in the village; Momus, Klamm’s village secretary, with the officials; Erlanger’s and Galater’s words reach K. only as messengers repeat them.

The introductory notes printed with the translation (Edwin Muir’s and Max Brod’s) read the Castle as divine grace, the reading Auden rejected in 1962. The piece takes from them only what they report: Kafka’s way with a sentence, the change from I to K., and the ending Kafka described.

If the lead can get the essay in full, the Title caption could stand on it.

From the examiner: in the Clauses tab Auden is now said only to cite the aphorism of the goal and the way, writing of a typical Kafka story. His own sentence there is about those the hero meets, and in this passage K. meets no one, so it was cut from that caption and kept in the view. remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md (conflicts left unresolved) records Mendelson’s remark that in 1941 Auden gave to The Castle an aphorism of Kafka’s that is not in it. Read at archive.org in Mendelson’s Early Auden, Later Auden (2017), p. 491: that is a different aphorism, on places of refuge and of salvation, so it does not touch this caption. Nothing on this page says the aphorism of the goal and the way is in the novel.

From the examiner: the German was read again at zeno.org (chapters 1, 2, 5 and 8) and bears out each thing the captions say of it. Two more departures of the Muirs’ that the list above does not have: where they have at every turn and double back, Kafka has always and a verb for steering in (the caption now says come round); and between the two street passages their K. is flatly unwilling to leave the street, where Kafka’s hesitates, evidently from tiredness.
